subject: infer binary latent variables with STAN?

messages.author: 4582a6b142da6b93
messages.subject: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
parts:
Dear Stan users and developers,

Hello. We are now working on a model (see below), where, for each object k, we wished to determine whether or not the object has a defect based on two attributes we measured for each object in our analysis (norm_Aff[k], and Acc[k], see below, highlighted in red). 

The variable norm_Aff[k] is the primary determinant and the Acc[k] is more secondary for the product defectiveness (greater values, better production quality), so in our model we made Acc as part of the prior for the binary latent variable delta[k], indicating whether or not one object is defective (0 is defective) 

In our study, we examined almost 10 millions of the objects,  and tested the model below using OpenBugs - it ran well well on a very small dataset (~100-500 objects), and gave very reasonable output, but the program took very long for the whole dataset, and eventually died. We have a very powerful cluster machine to do this computation, so I guess the problem should not be caused by memory/disk overflow etc.

My colleagues strongly recommended us to try STAN, as it is written in C and the sampling algorithms are more efficient than BUGs, so we were just wondering if STAN could handle this situation. We noticed in previous discussion that STAN might not directly accept discrete latent variables, and I am not sure if it is still the case. In our studies, a binary latent switch is extremely important in our modeling, so is there any workaround for this?

Thank you very much for your kind help, and we really appreciate it!!

Jorlen



model <- function() {
        for (k in 1:K){
                norm_Aff[k] ~ dnorm(mu[k], tau)
                mu[k] <- mu0 + w1*delta[k]
                delta[k] ~ dbern(p[k])
                p[k] <- Acc[k]*alpha
        }
        mu0 ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01)
        alpha ~ dbeta(1,1)
        w1 ~ dgamma(0.01,0.01)
        tau~dgamma(0.01,0.01)
}

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
parts:
On Wednesday, January 21, 2015 at 2:30:34 AM UTC-5, Jorlen Li wrote:
We noticed in previous discussion that STAN might not directly accept discrete latent variables, and I am not sure if it is still the case. In our studies, a binary latent switch is extremely important in our modeling, so is there any workaround for this?

In general, HMC requires derivatives to generate proposals for the unknowns and discrete unknowns are not differentiable. However, it is often possible to at least write down a conceptually equivalent model that only has continuous unknowns. In your case, I think you want to express your posterior distribution

f(delta, mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data)

as the product over k of

f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 0) * Pr(delta[k] = 0 | data) + 
f(mu0, alpha, w1, tau | data, delta[k] = 1) * Pr(delta[k] = 1 | data)

So, basically express your posterior distribution as a mixture of two posterior distributions with a Bernoulli mixing distribution. This is going to be a bit tedious because you have to loop over k and express the two components for each observation. Then, in the generated quantities block, you could draw from the posterior predictive distribution of the latent unknowns given the data.

Look in Chapter 9 (Finite Mixtures) of the Stan manual for more details and examples of how to do this.

Ben

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
parts:
If "latent switch" refers to something like a regression
parameter being "on" or "off", you can't really code that in
Stan.

I should add a negative example to the manual explaining why.
The short answer is the combinatorics of the marginalization
explode.

When the switch is like a mixture model on an observation
by observation or group-by-group level, it's much more
tractable to marginalize.

There's a new chapter in the manual directly on marginalization
out discrete parameters that don't directly look like
mixtures.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: infer binary latent variables with STAN?
parts:
There's no way to predict speed from size alone (even the size
of data plus size of parameters and knowledge of sparsity of data).
The form of the model along with the specific data set will determine
how well-behaved the posterior will be.

But even for simple models, MCMC won't be fast for 10M observations.
You might not be able to fit something that large for a complex
model using MCMC.

- Bob
